job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Rosa Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks, Rosa. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say is confidential, so give me your public view and your private one. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Busy, in a good way. I'm on a master's in cybersecurity at Lakeside, which is about protecting systems from attacks. I'm up at seven, in class by nine, and I use an AI assistant all day to explain things and check my code. In the evenings I build websites for small businesses, two clients right now, and I live at home with my parents and my grandmother, so dinner is loud.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What was your degree, and what did you do for your final project?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Information systems, passed with an average mark. My final project was a stock-tracking system for a family bakery, Marta's Ovens, and they still use it. I had no internship, since the places I applied to wanted someone with a year of experience for an internship, which made me laugh.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's about right, and honestly a bit of a relief. I use these tools every day and they're good, but they're not magic. They save me an hour or two a week and that's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine. My path, cybersecurity, stays in demand whether AI is hype or not, because attackers don't care about the hype. The real worry is that I'm average on paper and have a loan of about 9,500.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, get one professional certificate, and keep building sites for the two clients while I look for a security analyst job. I'd apply to banks and hospitals, since they always need that. I'd also ask Marta (the bakery owner) to recommend me to other shops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Slightly bored, honestly, which is a luxury problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the freelance work bring in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About 400 a month when it's going well, less in summer. It covers my phone, my train pass and a little for my gran's shopping. It also teaches me how to talk to customers who don't know what they want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you call yourself average if you're building real things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because employers read the grade first. My transcript says average, but the bakery's stock system has run for a year without a single crash, and I'd like people to read that first. I just have to find the people who do.

say: AI is **good** but not magic; it saves me an hour or two a week.
I'd say it's a **relief** that the hype was overblown.
think: Cybersecurity stays in **demand** whatever AI does.
My average grade and my **9,500 loan** are the real worry, much more than AI.
do: **Finish** the master's and earn one professional security certificate.
Keep building sites for my **two clients**.
**Apply** to banks and hospitals for security analyst jobs.
feel: **Fine**, slightly bored, which is a luxury problem.
S0.quote: My transcript says average, but the bakery's stock system has run for a year without a single crash, and I'd like people to read that first.
fieldNote: Adaptive and busy, she sees a plateau as **steady ground** for her chosen field.
Freelance work gives her about **400 a month** and client skills.
Wants employers to read her **projects** before her grade.

steps.text: Finish the master's and sit one security certificate exam
Keep maintaining two client websites for 400 a month
Apply for analyst jobs at banks and hospitals
Keep using AI to explain code and check my work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's exciting, and I'd mean it, but I'd add that it's uneven. Some of my classmates will get squeezed because they only do the easy parts. I'd post about which skills are safer, like understanding how attacks work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's good and bad. AI makes both attackers and defenders faster, so security work grows. But junior roles that check logs and write reports are exactly what tools take over, and that's the work a new graduate gets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd specialise early, in something like incident response where a person has to decide fast. I'd practise on public hacking challenges every week, and I'd keep my freelance work going. I'd also use AI to write my practice reports and then check every line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wired, in a mostly good way. A bit like the day before a big exam.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your classmates worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The ones who copy and paste from a chatbot and don't understand the answers. A friend of mine, Nico, passed the coding module that way, and he can't debug anything. If you can't tell when the machine is wrong, you're not an engineer, you're a messenger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Nico?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I already did. I said to build one thing from scratch every month, without the tool, just to keep the muscle. He said it's slow. I said that's the point.

say: It's **exciting** but uneven; some classmates will get squeezed.
Understanding **how attacks work** is a safer skill than only writing code.
think: Security work **grows**, but junior log-checking jobs are taken first.
The tools make both attackers and **defenders** faster.
do: **Specialise** early in incident response, where people decide fast.
feel: **Wired**, mostly in a good way, like the day before an exam.
S1.quote: If you can't tell when the machine is wrong, you're not an engineer, you're a messenger.
fieldNote: Sees change as **mixed**: new work for defenders, fewer junior chores.
Coaches a friend on **fundamentals**, which shows her teaching streak.
Her mood is lifted by **specialising** early.

steps.text: Do two public hacking challenges a week
Use AI to draft practice incident reports and check each line
Keep up the freelance clients and ask for referrals

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're not ready, and I'd say it plainly. Two years isn't enough for schools, banks or hospitals to change anything. I'd ask my local representative what the plan is for people who graduate in 2027.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be nervous, but I wouldn't freeze. Security might be one of the last jobs to go, since someone must watch the systems. Still, if thinking work is cheap, my entry job is at risk and the loan arrives at the worst time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any security or IT job as fast as I can, and I'd move my freelance work toward helping small shops protect themselves. I'd stay at home and save most of my income. And I'd start learning how robots and machines can be attacked, since that's the next thing that needs defending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A jolt. Like a cold shower, and then I'd start moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would small shops pay for protection in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because they'd be using tools they don't understand, and one mistake could close them. Marta's bakery has already had a scam email. When everything runs on software, the person who explains the risks in plain words becomes the most useful person in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your family think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My grandmother says work has always changed and we've always found a way. My mum is more worried, she's seen the news. I tell them I've a plan, and I'd better have one.

say: We're **not ready**; two years isn't enough for banks or hospitals.
I'd ask my representative what happens to **2027 graduates**.
think: Security may be one of the **last** jobs to go.
My entry job is at risk and the **loan** arrives at the worst time.
do: **Take** any security or IT job as fast as possible.
Shift **freelance** work toward protecting small shops.
**Save** most of my income and stay at home.
feel: A **jolt**, like a cold shower, then I'd start moving.
S2.quote: When everything runs on software, the person who explains the risks in plain words becomes the most useful person in the room.
fieldNote: Sees **protection** of small firms and machines as the next gap.
Family reaction splits between a **calm grandmother** and a worried mother.

steps.text: Apply for any security or IT support job immediately
Offer small shops a basic security check for a monthly fee
Save most of the income while living at home
Write to my representative about help for graduates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a window, and the smart thing is to use it. I'd tell classmates to find the skill that's hardest to copy, which for me is judgement under pressure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel okay. I'd have a first job, two or three years of experience, and savings before the real change. I'd probably already be in a security team that's using AI heavily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get a job at a bank or hospital security team and put 300 a month into savings. I'd finish the loan early and build a small business on the side, helping shops. And I'd learn about robot and machine security once the date gets close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Positive. A bit of fear is there to keep me sharp.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does judgement under pressure look like in security?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the 3 a.m. call when something's leaking and you have to decide whether to shut a hospital system down. A tool can suggest. A person must decide and sign. I'd rather be the person who makes the call than the person who reads what a program recommends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the thought of AGI change how you spend?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. I'd stop buying a new phone every two years and put that money toward the loan. It's small, but it adds up. And I'd tell my brother to do the same.

say: Five years is a **window**; use it wisely.
Find the **skill** that's hardest to copy, like judgement under pressure.
think: I'd have a first job and **savings** before the real change.
I'd likely work in a **security team** that uses AI heavily.
do: **Join** a bank or hospital security team.
**Put** 300 a month into savings and clear the loan early.
feel: **Positive**, with a little fear to keep me sharp.
S3.quote: I'd rather be the person who makes the call than the person who reads what a program recommends.
fieldNote: Her adaptivity and a **specialist field** make a five-year window feel useful.
Wants to be the person who **decides**, not the one who reads.
Small **money habits** reflect a plan, not panic.

steps.text: Join a bank or hospital security team within a year
Put 300 a month into savings and repay the loan early
Run a small shop security service on the side
Study robot and machine security as the date nears

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time to get ready, so there's no excuse. I'd tell people to build skills that mix tech with people, like security or health.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel good. By 34 I could lead a security team or run my own small firm, with real savings and maybe a place of my own. I'd probably be using AI the whole way and still be useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd climb in a security team for five years, then think about starting a firm. I'd buy a flat in Lakeside with a partner or alone. And I'd study one new area every year, so I'm never the last to hear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and quite happy. It's a nice view.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would keep you from getting too comfortable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The yearly study habit, and my friends. Nico and I swap what we've learnt every few months. I trust a friend who tells me my skills are stale more than any ten-year plan I could write.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any scenario in which this ten years goes badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the change comes sooner than the card says, or if my grandmother needs more care and money goes there. I'd still be fine, but my plan would bend. I'm okay with bending.

say: Ten years is **long** enough to prepare, so no excuses.
Build skills that mix **tech with people**, like security or health care.
think: By 34 I could lead a **security team** or run my own firm.
AI will be everywhere and I'll still be **useful**.
do: **Climb** in a security team for five years, then think about a firm.
**Buy** a flat in Lakeside once savings allow.
feel: **Calm** and quite happy, with a nice view.
S4.quote: I trust a friend who tells me my skills are stale more than any ten-year plan I could write.
fieldNote: Adaptive habits and a long window leave her **confident**.
Relies on friends as a **reality check**, not just a plan.
Accepts that a family **care need** could bend her plans.

steps.text: Climb in a security team for five years, then consider a firm
Save for a flat deposit in Lakeside
Study one new security area every year
Set aside a care fund in case Grandma needs more help

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because the loan and the first job would collide with the change. What would help is a graduate guarantee, such as a paid first-year placement, and clear support for people who can't adapt as fast as I do.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe that adapting is easier with family around. I can try ten things a month because Mum cooks dinner and my grandmother keeps the house calm, and not everyone has that.

headlineQuote: I can try ten things a month because Mum cooks dinner and my grandmother keeps the house calm, and not everyone has that.
portrait: Rosa is 24, doing a **cybersecurity** master's after a pass in information systems.
She lives with her parents and grandmother in **Lakeside** and builds sites for two clients.
Centrist and adaptive, she uses AI **every day** and treats change as something to ride.
Her bet is **specialising**, so she is the person who makes the call under pressure.
She owes about 9,500, and her mood is calm to **anxious** depending on the timeline.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most, because the loan and first job collide with it.
whatWouldHelp: A **graduate guarantee** such as a paid first-year placement, plus support for slower adapters.
